text_blocks.snippet: The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends annual lung cancer screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) for adults aged 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years. This recommendation is based on evidence that LDCT screening can reduce lung cancer mortality in this high-risk population.
snippet_highlighted_words: annual lung cancer screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) for adults aged 50 to 80 years who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years

list.snippet: Smoking History: 20 pack-years or more. A pack-year is calculated by multiplying the number of packs of cigarettes smoked per day by the number of years a person has smoked.
Smoking Status: Currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years.

list.title: Annual Screening:
list.snippet: The USPSTF recommends annual lung cancer screening with low-dose CT for individuals meeting the above criteria.

list.title: Shared Decision Making:
list.snippet: The decision to undergo screening should be made after a discussion between the individual and their healthcare provider, considering the potential benefits, limitations, and harms of screening.

list.title: Discontinuation of Screening:
list.snippet: Screening should be discontinued once a person has not smoked for 15 years or if they develop a health problem that limits their life expectancy or ability to undergo lung surgery.

list.title: Reduced Mortality:
list.snippet: Studies have shown that LDCT screening can significantly reduce lung cancer mortality in high-risk individuals.

list.title: Early Detection:
list.snippet: LDCT can detect lung cancer at an earlier stage, when treatment is more likely to be successful.

list.title: Harms of Screening:
list.snippet: While LDCT screening can be beneficial, it also carries potential harms, such as false-positive results, unnecessary follow-up tests, and radiation exposure.

list.title: Shared Decision Making:
list.snippet: It is crucial for individuals to discuss the potential benefits and harms of screening with their healthcare provider to make an informed decision.

list.title: Access to Screening:
list.snippet: Ensuring access to screening services, especially for individuals in underserved populations, is essential to maximize the benefits of these recommendations.

list.title: Continued Research:
list.snippet: Ongoing research is needed to further refine screening strategies and address disparities in screening uptake and outcomes.
